title: Meta Fires 8,000 While Spending $145 Billion on AI — and India's IT Industry Is Paying the Price
excerpt: The biggest tech layoffs of 2026 collide with a historic crash in Indian IT valuations, leaving hundreds of thousands of diaspora workers caught between Silicon Valley's pivot and Bengaluru's anxiety
body:
## The Great Rebalancing

When Mark Zuckerberg told Meta's 80,000 employees in late April that the company would shed 8,000 of them by May 20, the internal reaction was not shock so much as exhaustion. This was, after all, the third major round of layoffs in less than four years — but the first in which the company openly admitted the cuts were designed to fund artificial intelligence, not merely trim pandemic-era excess.

Meta's 2026 capital expenditure guidance now stands at a staggering $145 billion, the vast majority earmarked for AI infrastructure: data centres, custom chips, and the compute power required to deliver what Zuckerberg calls "personal super-intelligence" for the platform's 3.9 billion monthly active users. The human cost of that ambition landed on a single Monday.

## A Familiar Playbook, a New Pretext

The mechanics are grimly familiar. Affected staff received 16 weeks of base pay plus two weeks per year of service. Internal message boards, according to former employees, descended into a "doomsday mood" in the days before, with workers photographing free snacks and chargers as mementos of a soon-to-be-former life. More unsettling were reports of AI-powered monitoring software tracking employee productivity — a tool whose existence, Meta conceded, was part of its push to identify roles that could be automated.

Meta is not alone. Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to 8,750 staff in the same week. Oracle cut 30,000. Across the sector, 132,000 tech workers have lost their jobs in 2026 so far. But Meta's layoffs carry an outsized symbolic weight: the company that once promised to connect the world is now openly replacing the people who built those connections with the machines they trained.

## The Indian IT Aftershock

Six thousand kilometres from Menlo Park, the tremors are arguably more severe. India's $260-billion IT services industry — the backbone of middle-class aspiration for a generation — is staring at a reckoning. The Nifty IT index has plunged to a three-year low, with bellwethers Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, and HCL Technologies each shedding between three and five per cent in a single session after OpenAI announced a $4-billion enterprise AI venture that threatens to automate precisely the back-office coding, testing, and maintenance work that Indian firms sell to Fortune 500 clients.

Analysts at Kotak Institutional Equities have drawn the starkest comparison yet: Indian IT valuations, they argue, are approaching levels last seen during the 2008 subprime crisis. The sector's price-to-earnings ratio has compressed from 28x a year ago to under 19x today. Revenue growth guidance from TCS and Infosys for the current fiscal year came in well below Street expectations, and hiring freezes are the norm rather than the exception.

## The Diaspora in the Crosshairs

For the estimated 300,000-plus Indian-origin workers at American technology firms, the layoffs are not an abstraction. H-1B visa holders face a 60-day window to find new employment or leave the country — a bureaucratic guillotine that turns every pink slip into an immigration crisis. Reports have surfaced of laid-off Meta employees scrambling to file transfer petitions on the same day they lost their badges.

The anxiety extends beyond Silicon Valley. In Bengaluru and Hyderabad, where Indian IT companies employ roughly four million people, engineers who once considered their jobs recession-proof are updating résumés and enrolling in AI certification programmes. Nasscom, the industry body, has taken to releasing cautiously optimistic projections about AI "creating new roles," but the mood on engineering floors is sceptical.

## What Comes Next

The irony is structural. Meta is spending $145 billion on AI partly because firms like TCS and Infosys proved that software work could be offshored and commoditised. AI is simply the next iteration of that logic — offshoring to machines rather than countries. Indian IT leaders insist they can ride the wave: Infosys CEO Salil Parekh has spoken of "AI-first delivery models," and Wipro has retrained 45,000 engineers in generative AI tools.

Whether retraining can outrun automation remains the trillion-dollar question. For now, the clearest signal is in the markets. Investors are pricing Indian IT as though the best days are behind it — and pricing Meta as though the best days are being bought, one layoff at a time.

*Sources: Meta corporate communications; Kotak Institutional Equities; Outlook Business; Reuters; PeopleMatters; Nasscom FY26 Strategic Review.*
